**OIG issued the most recommendations in 2015: 1,914.** The data is current as of 2026-11-04 and isn't stale.

**Runners-up:**
- 2014: 1,670
- 2013: 1,394
- 2020: 1,211
- 2017: 1,152

**Other context:**
- **Status of the 2015 recommendations:** 1,903 were closed as implemented and 11 were closed as not implemented. None are still open. The median time to close was 227 days.

**Reading the trend:** The counts fell after the 2013–2015 peak and settled at roughly 600–1,200 a year. That could mean facilities had fewer problems. It could also reflect changes in inspection protocols, how many reports OIG published, or where OIG focused its attention. These numbers alone can't tell those apart.

**Completeness:** This copy of the data has 15,649 recommendations. OIG's dashboard reports 15,778, a difference of 129, which is within the accepted margin. The totals by year may therefore be slightly low.

**No. By this measure, suicide-related recommendations fell sharply from 2024 to 2025. But the drop seems to come mostly from a change in how OIG inspects facilities, so it doesn't show that suicide prevention got better or that OIG cares less about it.**

Data as of 2026-11-04 (current, not stale).

**The counts**

| Year | Reports with a recommendation mentioning "suicide" | Recommendations mentioning "suicide" | All reports with recommendations | Share of reports |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2024 | **56** | 98 | 155 | about 36% |
| 2025 | **11** | 19 | 132 | about 8% |

For context: 2020 had 23 reports, 2021 had 34, 2022 had 10, 2023 had 32, and 2026 has 10 so far (partial year). The 2024 count is the highest of the period. It isn't the start of a rising trend.

**What's behind the drop**

The type of report changed between the two years:
- **2024:** 55 of the 98 recommendations came from the Comprehensive Healthcare Inspection Program, OIG's older routine facility inspections, which regularly checked suicide-related items. Hotline inspections (18), Vet Center inspections (15), national reviews (8) and mental health inspections (2) made up the rest.
- **2025:** None came from that older program. Its replacement, the current Healthcare Facility Inspection program, also produced none in 2025. The 19 came from mental health inspections (9), Vet Center inspections (5), national reviews (3) and hotline inspections (2).

So the drop matches the switch in inspection programs. Suicide findings may now show up through a different route, the mental health inspections. That's an inference from the report types, not something OIG has said.

**What these counts can show**
- How many published reports had at least one recommendation using the word "suicide," by year, compared with all reports that had recommendations.
- That in 2025, suicide wording appeared mainly in mental health and Vet Center inspections, not routine facility inspections.

**What they cannot show**
- **Whether VA got better or worse at suicide prevention.** A falling count could mean problems were fixed. It could also mean inspection methods, the number of reports, or OIG's focus changed. The program switch makes the second reading at least as likely here.
- **How much OIG cares about the topic.** A report only counts if a *recommendation* contains the word. Reports that reviewed suicide prevention and found nothing wrong, or put it only in the report text, aren't counted.
- **Everything related to suicide.** This is a word match. Recommendations about safety planning, risk screening, lethal means or patient safety checks that never say "suicide" are missed. I'm also not sure whether words like "suicidal" were matched. OIG's own "Suicide Prevention" topic label isn't a reliable alternative, because only about a quarter of reports have any topic label.
- **How serious the problems were.** Every recommendation counts the same, and a report with one suicide-related recommendation counts the same as a report with five.
- **Whether recommendations are still open.** Newer years naturally have more open items (2025 has 6 of 19 open), so don't compare open or closed status across years.

If you want, I can list the individual 2024 and 2025 reports with their report numbers and links, or search for related wording (such as safety planning or lethal means) to give a broader picture.

**Median: 179 days, or about 6 months.** That figure covers Veterans Benefits Administration (VBA) recommendations in OIG's published record. The data is current as of 2026-11-04 and isn't stale.

**What the number measures**
It's the time from when OIG published the report to when OIG marked the recommendation closed. It is not the time VBA took to do the work. The closure date appears to record when OIG closed the recommendation after reviewing VBA's evidence, which can be months after the fix itself. So treat 179 days as the time to get a recommendation closed through OIG's review.

**The numbers**
- **Recommendations naming VBA:** 966 in total. 923 are closed (897 implemented, 26 closed as not implemented, a 2.8% rate) and 43 are open.
- **Sample behind the median:** 914 closed recommendations. A few closed ones have no closure date on OIG's site; across all offices that's about 6% of closures, mostly from 2013–2016.
- **Middle half:** most closed within 134 to 312.5 days, so many took 4½ to 10+ months.
- **Closed the day the report came out:** 110 recommendations, presumably fixed before publication. They pull the median down a little.
- **Still open:** the typical open item is 161 days old, 17 have been open more than a year, and the oldest is 1,567 days (about 4.3 years).

**Things to keep in mind**
- The count includes any recommendation that names VBA, including ones assigned jointly to another office. A recommendation naming two offices counts for both. That's why the results also show small groups for Information and Technology (11 recommendations, median 330 days) and the Veterans Health Administration (5, median 71 days).
- Only 7 VBA recommendations have a target date the tool could read. All 7 closed after their target. That doesn't mean VBA missed deadlines: a target is the office's own estimate, and OIG's closure date can come months after the work was done.

Source: VA OIG recommendations data (https://www.vaoig.gov/recommendations-all). These are totals across many reports, so no single report number applies. I can break the trend down by year or look at specific reports if that would help.

It appears in **21 of the 112 inspection reports** in scope, about 19%. **The VA El Paso Healthcare System is not in that group.** This is based on data as of **2026-11-04**, which is current.

**The top finding (cluster 260)**
- **What it says:** The Chief of Staff and Associate Director for Patient Care Services should create workflows showing how each team member takes part in communicating test results. The standard is VHA Directive 1088(1), *Communicating Test Results to Providers and Patients*.
- **How common:** 26 recommendations across 21 of 112 reports, all published in 2026. 17 of the 26 are still open.

El Paso's latest inspection is report **25-00193-155** (on site January 14–16, 2025; published July 16, 2026). Two other common findings also concern cleanliness: cluster 262, "maintain a clean environment to reduce the risk of infection" (11 of 112 reports), and cluster 264, "keep patient care areas clean and safe" (9 of 112). So El Paso shares this cleanliness issue with other facilities, though its recommendation is filed in a separate group.
2. **Complete secondary toxic exposure screenings within 30 days.** This one isn't in any recurring-finding group. The facility says it currently has none overdue and has started monthly reporting to its Clinical Executive Council.

The facility record shows no repeat findings for El Paso. A repeat means the same standard recommendation appeared in more than one of its reports, and only recommendations in a group are compared.

- The groups are built from recommendations with matching or similar wording. A shared group suggests a common issue but doesn't prove a common cause.

- **Recommendation:** Secure medication carts when not in use, and have managers monitor compliance.
- **What the facility committed to:**
  - Physically checked every medication cart ("Flow Cart") in six patient areas and confirmed the locks and other security parts worked.
  - Retrained staff on the two cited units, with sign‑in sheets as proof.
  - Nurse managers would check that carts were secured on rounds before noon each business day, and clinical nurse leaders would make random weekly checks.
  - Weekly facility‑wide environment of care (safety) rounds would record cart checks. Problems would be tracked and trended and reported each quarter to the Environment of Care Committee.
- **Target date:** Sept 30, 2015. **Closed:** Sept 22, 2015.
- Link: https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/comprehensive-healthcare-inspection-program/combined-assessment-program-review-west-palm-2

- **Recommendation:** Strengthen processes so medication carts are secured at all times, and monitor compliance.
- **What the facility committed to:**
  - Some carts had locks that didn't work, so it repaired or replaced them. Six new carts had arrived, 26 more were on order, and the rest were being purchased.
  - Until then, carts would stay in a locked medication room when not in use.

- **Target date:** Dec 31, 2014. **Closed:** March 11, 2015.

## 3. Problems OIG found but fixed before the report (be ready if they look again)
The 2026 report lists four problems that were fixed by December 2025, so OIG didn't make recommendations for them. Inspectors may still check that the fixes held:
- Clean equipment stored in soiled utility rooms in the primary care and women's health clinics (VHA Directive 1131)
- Expired respirator masks in a locked clean storage room that Environment of Care rounds hadn't checked in six months
- An emergency alert system at an outpatient clinic that could only be reset from inside the police station

## 4. What OIG commonly finds at other facilities (current inspection program)

- Keeping a clean environment to reduce infection risk (VHA Directive 1608(1)): **11 of 112**, all 11 still open

- Groups of similar findings are based on matching wording. They suggest a shared issue but don't prove a common cause, and one theme can be split across several groups.
- Target dates are each facility's own estimate. They aren't a measure of missed deadlines.
- In the data, the IT report is tagged as VISN 1 rather than VISN 17. That looks like a labeling error and doesn't change the findings.

**Why there's no ranking**
- OIG inspects facilities on a rotating schedule and looks into specific complaints. Each report covers one facility, at one point in time, on the topics that review chose. Two reports usually can't be compared on equal terms.
- How many recommendations a facility has isn't a measure of quality. It depends on how often OIG reviewed it, what kind of review it was (a broad inspection or a narrow hotline case), and when. A facility reviewed more often will tend to have more findings.
- The tools I have here can report the record, but they're built not to rate facilities, and their counting tool can't group results by facility.

2. **Problems that come up across the system:** which findings recur across many facilities and how long they usually take to fix.
3. **Patterns by region or topic:** counts, closure times and open-item aging grouped by year, office, topic or report type, filtered by state or VISN (VA's regional networks).

**Nobody can say exactly what OIG will cite El Paso for next time.** OIG doesn't publish its findings in advance or its inspection schedule. But the public record shows where El Paso's risk is highest. (Data as of 2026-11-04; current, not stale.)

## When the next inspection might be (estimate only)
Around **January 2028**. That's just El Paso's last inspection (Healthcare Facility Inspection, ended 2025-01-16) plus about three years, which is the program's usual cycle. OIG publishes no schedule, so this is not a known date.

## 1. El Paso's own open recommendations (most likely to be checked)
El Paso has 19 reports and 66 recommendations on record, and **4 are still open**:

**From the last inspection, report [25-00193-155](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-el-paso-healthcare-system)** (published 2026-07-16):
- **Clean and safe environment (Rec 1).** Target date 2027-01-29. The facility's plan includes daily cleaning by housekeeping (Environmental Management Services) with restroom logs, 24 new cleaning procedures, staff training finished June 2, 2026, daily oversight by the housekeeping chief, and weekly rounds by the Associate Director. The same report also noted several problems that were fixed before OIG wrote it up, so OIG made no recommendation on them:
  - clean and dirty items stored together
  - expired respirator masks in a storage room that inspection teams couldn't get into
  - an emergency alarm whose reset button was in the locked police station
  - a damaged restroom floor
- **Secondary toxic exposure screenings finished within 30 days (Rec 2).** Target date 2026-12-31. As of June 2026 none were overdue. A written procedure was still being drafted, and the goal is zero overdue screenings for six months in a row, reported monthly to the Clinical Executive Council.

**From the information security inspection, report [23-01179-204](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/information-security-inspection/inspection-information-security-va-el-paso-healthcare)** (published 2023-09-27), both still open after about three years:
- Working, monitored video surveillance for the data center (Rec 5)
- Water detection sensors in the data center (Rec 7)

**Repeat findings:** none on record. That means OIG hasn't issued the same standard recommendation to El Paso in more than one report. Only recommendations that fall into a group of similar findings get compared, and a repeat would mean the issue was cited again, not that nothing was done in between.

## 2. Most common findings at other facilities under the current program
These are ranked by how often they show up, not by how serious they are, and they don't predict what El Paso's inspection will find.

| Finding theme | How common | Typical time to close |
|---|---|---|
| Written workflows for telling providers and patients about test results (VHA Directive 1088) | 21 of 112 reports | median 0 days (only 9 closed) |
| Test-result policy and workflows that meet VHA rules, plus tracking that patients are notified | 12 of 112 | median 256 days |
| Clean environment to reduce infection risk (VHA Directive 1608) | 11 of 112 | median 0 days (only 3 closed) |
| Network (VISN) leaders ensuring stable facility leadership | 9 of 112 | median 237 days |
| Patient care areas kept clean and safe | 9 of 112 | median 191.5 days |
| Test-result workflows for each service | 9 of 112 | median 139 days |
| Expired supplies and clean supply areas | 6 of 112 | median 230.5 days |
| Tracking whether providers tell patients about abnormal test results | 6 of 112 | median 238 days |

How to read this:
- **Test-result communication is the most common theme**, even though it's split across four of the groups above. El Paso doesn't appear in any of them. That doesn't prove El Paso was never cited for it, and it doesn't mean El Paso is fine there.
- **Cleanliness is a common theme too, and it matches El Paso's own open Rec 1.** It doesn't appear in those two cleanliness groups only because the tool groups findings by wording, and El Paso's wording landed in a different group.
- **The "0 days" medians are misleading.** Few of those findings have closed, and ones closed on the day the report came out pull the median down.

## Practical takeaway
- Show proof that the cleanliness and toxic exposure screening fixes are holding.
- Close out the two data center items from 2023.
- Check your test-result workflows against VHA Directive 1088 now, since that's what OIG cites most often at other facilities.

For model fixes, the reports above show what other facilities committed to, for example Louisville ([24-03205-235](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-louisville-healthcare)) and Walla Walla ([24-00599-202](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-jonathan-m-wainwright)).

I can pull the full text of any of these reports or look deeper into a specific area if that would help.
